title: SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The refinement rule is mathematically inconsistent for odd k. The paper says it “enforce[s] that at least half” of k selected concepts are shared, but then specifies selecting shared concepts only until floor(k/2). For k=5, floor(5/2)=2, which is fewer than half under the stated requirement; the following sentence instead says that in practice it ensures at least 3 shared concepts. The algorithm must use ceil(k/2), or the stated guarantee must be revised.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, “Multimodal Graph Refinement,” definition of F
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The graph-refinement score requires F, described as “the set of video frames containing the object state.” But Sections 3.1 and 4.1 state that training videos have only video-level action labels and lack frame-level state annotations. The paper never explains how F is obtained without unavailable ground-truth state-frame labels (for example, whether it is derived from the pseudo labels). As written, the refinement procedure requires supervision that the paper claims not to have, or leaves an essential leakage-sensitive step unspecified.

The reported deltas imply incompatible complete-model scores within the same column. “W/o Visual Descriptions” is 48.4 with -7.0, implying a full-model score of 55.4. But “W/o Joint Training” is 47.9 with -4.1, implying 52.0, and “W/o Dynamic State Locating” is 48.8 with -3.2, also implying 52.0. These cannot all be differences from one complete model as claimed by the caption.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, “Novel Objects and Actions,” versus Table 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 says that prior work “(Souček et al., 2022, 2024; Xue et al., 2024) trains separate specialized models for different objects or actions.” This directly conflicts with the paper’s own Table 1, which labels MTC (Souček et al., 2024) as a unified model (✓), and with the preceding baseline description that says “MTC trains a unified model for all objects and actions given a known vocabulary.” The characterization of the 2024 Souček work must be corrected.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction final paragraph; Conclusion; Table A9
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims SAGE “outperforms the prior state-of-the-art ... across all benchmarks” and later “outperforms all baselines.” Its own Table A9 does not support a general superiority claim over VidOSC: e.g., SAGE vs. VidOSC has p=0.27 for ChangeIt State Pre@1, p=1.0 for ChangeIt open-world transitioning Pre@1 (seen), p=1.0 for HowToChange F1 (seen), p=0.35 for HowToChange precision (seen), and p=0.093 for HowToChange F1 (novel). Several corresponding Table 1/Table 7 values are equal or only numerically marginal. Given the paper’s own stated p<0.05 criterion, broad claims of outperforming VidOSC/all baselines must be qualified to the metrics/settings with demonstrated significance.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sections 3.2–3.3 and Section 4.1 claim that SAGE uses no privileged object/action information
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed action/object-free inference nevertheless requires a prebuilt SAGE containing candidate objects and candidate actions. Inference explicitly evaluates “each object o” in SAGE and then “all actions potentially associated with the identified object”; construction of a node for a novel action/object requires that novel action/object name. Thus open-world test-time operation necessarily depends on a candidate vocabulary/graph containing the held-out classes. The paper states that it “always infers these labels from videos without privileged access,” but does not disclose how the held-out object/action candidate names and their graph nodes are made available, or whether they are derived from test-set label vocabularies. This is essential for assessing whether the open-world protocol uses privileged class information.
